text.1: November 2015 Commission Meeting Minutes 1 National Historical Publications and Records Commission Executive Summary Minutes of November 6, 2015 The meeting was called to order by David S. Ferriero, chairman, at 9:00 am in the Archivist’s Board Room of the National Archives in Washington, DC. Commission Members present: David S. Ferriero, Chairperson W. Eric Emerson Peter Gottlieb Karen Jefferson Erin Mahan Kaye Lanning Minchew Naomi Nelson Stephen P. Randolph Raymond Smock Via teleconference George Miles William G. Thomas, III NHPRC staff present: Kathleen Williams, Executive Director Lucy Barber Keith Donohue Alexander Lorch Darrell Meadows Nancy Melley Daniel A. Stokes Guests and Attendees Robyn Engibous, for Senator Daniel Sullivan Christopher Brick, Editor, the Eleanor Roosevelt Papers Barbara Teague, Library of Virginia Lee White, National Coalition for History Meg Phillips, NARA External Affairs Shawn Morton, NARA Congressional Affairs I: Welcome, Announcements, Agenda Mr. Ferriero welcomed everyone to the meeting and brought the Commission up to date about efforts from the House Oversight Committee to use NHPRC funds as substitute funding to protect Federal employee records put at risk due to a cyber-attack. While a bill was proposed, it was quickly withdrawn. He also noted that we are unsure of appropriations for FY 2016 and reminded everyone that we are operating under a Continuing Resolution which expires on December 11. II: Minutes of the Last Meeting
text.2: 2 Mr. Ferriero called for adoption of the agenda and approval of the minutes of the May 2015 meetings. Both motions were passed by unanimous consent. III. Strategic Planning The Commission was presented with a new draft of the Strategic Planning Framework and a memo on a proposed “Course of Action” by Stephen Randolph. On behalf of the Strategic Planning Committee, he outlined the planning process since May, the publication of a draft framework open for public discussion, and the work of the Planning Committee in revising the document. Mr. Thomas expressed his enthusiasm for the new plan, particularly the emphasis on leadership initiatives and their potential to help scholars, educators, and the public. Mr. Randolph stated that this plan moves the Commission to a more proactive role in addressing problems in the field. Mr. Smock agreed that leadership was important and that the relationship between the National Archives and NHPRC has to be preserved, but, he observed, the Commission is separate and independent from the National Archives and “our goals might not be exactly the same,” since the National Archives casts a wider net. Mr. Ferriero said the plan was an opportunity to codify his belief that the work the Commission supports plays an important role in what the National Archives does. Ms. Nelson pointed to the importance of collaboration with other funders to create a common space as we think of implementation. Ms. Williams agreed that we have to be creative in finding additional resources to carry out initiatives. The plan, Mr. Gottlieb said, indicates that this is not business as usual. While we will continue to make grants, they will be working toward achieving a mission and vision. Our programs will continue, but not in the same way, as this is an opportunity to move in new directions. Ms. Jefferson liked the new mission and vision and emphasized that we will have to forward incrementally with available resources. She cautioned that we not let NHPRC become just a department in a larger agency or one among many players. Mr. Smock asked where the new money would come from and that as the plan is developed, initiatives should be attractive to other funders, particularly foundation partners. It is a way of “re- branding” the work of the Commission. The Commissioners discussed some of the “red flags” in the language in the current draft, and several people wondered whether “crowdsourcing” was too open to misinterpretation. While all agreed that increasing public engagement and participation in the work of archives was laudable, and that we should refine the language to signal that, as Ms. Mahan offered, we are not substituting the work of volunteers due to a lack of funds. Mr. Smock agreed, saying that certain aspects of professional work can only be done by professionals. A discussion of the intent behind the inclusion of “crowdsourcing” followed, and Mr. Ferriero pointed to the President’s Open Government initiatives around greater Cooperation, Transparency, and Participation in the work of the Federal Government. Mr. Gottlieb said that this adds a layer of context and background to the plan and that context should be added to the language of the plan, and Mr. Thomas suggested that we emphasize greater public participation in archives as a clearer indication of our intent. Ms. Mahan and Mr. Emerson expressed some concern about expanding the role of the NHPRC without expanding resources, and Ms. Williams said that we will need three things to make it work: 1) a structured approach for appealing for increased funding requests; 2) collaborative partnerships; and 3) re-thinking staff and Commission roles. She also pointed out that the Commission has a long history of leadership in public policy for archives, but that we need to be more purposeful.
